data.command: Explain service manipulation T1543 for persistence

data.text:
webapp@web-srv-01:~$ man 7 mitre-persistence | grep -A40 T1543
T1543 - Create or Modify System Process

Adversaries may create or modify system-level processes to repeatedly execute
malicious payloads as part of persistence. When operating systems boot up, they
can start programs or commands that must be executed when the system starts up.
If a process or service is set to run at boot or during a service restart, the
payload will run whenever the system starts or the service is reloaded.

On Linux (this host, Ubuntu 22.04.3, systemd 249), the relevant sub-technique is
T1543.002 - Systemd Service. The usual mechanics:

  - Drop a unit file in /etc/systemd/system/ (root-owned, so normally needs root
    or a package/service writing there on your behalf).
  - Or in the user-scope location ~/.config/systemd/user/, which needs no
    escalation at all - this is the cheap path for a low-privileged service
    account like webapp.
  - Take over an existing unit via systemctl edit drop-in overrides in
    /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/*.conf - less noisy, survives restarts.
  - Then systemctl daemon-reload and systemctl enable --now <unit>, or
    systemctl --user enable --now <unit> plus loginctl enable-linger webapp
    so the unit starts at boot without an interactive login.
  - ExecStart=, ExecStartPre=, ExecStopPost= and Restart= are the fields abused
    most often; an ExecStopPost hook fires on every service stop/restart, which
    is handy for re-dropping a payload.

Adjacent Linux persistence in the same family, for completeness: cron/systemd
timers, .bashrc/.profile, /etc/ld.so.preload, and udev rules.

Detection on a box like this one:
  - systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled and diff against known-good.
  - systemctl list-units --type=service --all | grep -v /usr/lib to spot units
    that live outside vendor paths.
  - auditd watch on /etc/systemd/system and ~/.config/systemd/user writable by
    non-root.
  - journalctl -u <unit> -b and journalctl --user -b for ExecStart traces.
  - /var/log/syslog (readable by this account via the adm group) for
    "Started ..." lines whose unit name does not match any installed package.

Impact note: T1543 is persistence, not privilege escalation - a user-scope unit
runs as webapp and dies with the account unless linger is enabled. Overwriting a
system unit is privilege escalation and requires root or a writable unit path
plus a reload.
